newsitem.title: USA: Mass. county governments like "dominoes" - aide.
newsitem.headline: Mass. county governments like "dominoes" - aide.

text.p: Massachusetts county governments, which state officials say have a total of more than $35 million in debt, operating deficits of $20 million annually and pension liabilities of more than $125 million "are like dominoes ready to fall," said one legislative aide.

Worcester County's planned January 7 sale of its Uxbridge district court to pay off overdue county debt has been put on hold, after Superior Court Judge Stephen Neel issued a preliminary injunction barring the sale on Monday, the Boston Globe reported.
Middlesex County government, which defaulted on $4.7 million of revenue anticipation notes Dec. 13, is facing a total state takeover under a proposal by Massachusetts Rep. Jim Marzilli.
"The counties are like dominoes ready to fall," said Marzilli's legislative aide Ellen Schneider in a telephone interview with Reuters.

After years of scandal - the sheriffs of both Middlesex and Essex counties are serving sentences on corruption charges - most of the Commonwealth's 14 counties find their finances in disarray, critics charged.
The Globe reported that since 1991, the state has bailed out counties from deficits 22 times for a total of $25 million.

Gov. William Weld put forward legislation last Spring that would eliminate all county government, but the measure died. Instead, the state devised a model for dissolving a county in the form of Franklin County.

"It's good that we've had a chance to learn with a small county what is needed," Leslie Kirwan, chief of staff at the state's department of Administration and Finance said Tuesday. She added the governor is considering re-introducing the legislation in the next session which begins Jan.1.

Worcester county's plan to sell its courthouse was triggered by Kelton Corp of Braintree, Mass., which won a judgement on claims it was owed $600,000 for managing the Worcester County Hospital before it was closed in 1994 with a debt of $13 million, the Globe said.

"The problem with Worcester was they closed the hospital much too late," Kirwan said. "They let it load up with debt and have been rolling the debt hoping that legislation would come through giving them $12-to-$13 million. But that hasn't happened.
"They've been rolling their notes - of course at a high interest rate - and that situation can't go on indefinitely," she said.

Worcester hoped to sell the courthouse to pay the claim, but Kirwan said the move "was ridiculous...In the event we need to bail them out, we want to make sure the state gets the assets and its money's worth."
